content: Gunnera is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants, some of which are remarkably large in size. It is the sole genus within the family Gunneraceae. The genus comprises approximately 40 to 50 species, which exhibit significant variation in leaf size. Among these, Gunnera manicata, native to the Serra do Mar mountain range in southeastern Brazil, is considered one of the largest species.5 to 2 meters (5 to 6 feet) in width, but in exceptional cases, they can grow up to 3.4 meters (11 feet) wide. These leaves are supported by thick, succulent petioles (leaf stalks) that can reach lengths of up to 2.5 meters (8 feet). Optimal germination for this species occurs in very moist, but not waterlogged, conditions, with temperatures ranging from 22 to 29°C. Another large species, Gunnera masafuerae, is native to the Juan Fernández Islands off the coast of Chile. This species can produce leaves up to 2.9 meters (9 feet 5 inches) wide, supported by robust petioles that are 1.5 meters (5 feet) long and 11 centimeters (4.5 inches) thick, as documented by Skottsberg. On the nearby Isla Más Afuera, Gunnera peltata often develops an upright trunk that can grow up to 5.5 meters (18 feet) tall and 25–30 centimeters (10–12 inches) thick, with leaves reaching widths of up to 2 meters (6 feet 4 inches). In the Colombian Andes, Gunnera magnifica is notable for producing the largest leaf buds of any known plant, measuring up to 60 centimeters (2 feet) in length and 40 centimeters (16 inches) in thickness. Its succulent petioles can grow up to 2.7 meters (8 feet 10 inches) long. This species also produces a massive inflorescence of small, reddish flowers, which can reach lengths of 2.3 meters (7 feet 6 inches) and weigh approximately 13 kilograms. Other giant species of Gunnera are distributed across the Neotropics and Hawaii. In contrast, smaller species are found in regions such as New Zealand and South America. For example, Gunnera albocarpa from New Zealand has leaves that are only 1–2 centimeters long, while Gunnera magellanica from South America has leaves measuring 5–9 centimeters wide, supported by petioles 8–15 centimeters long. The genus is commonly referred to as giant rhubarb. It was named in honor of the Norwegian botanist Johann Ernst Gunnerus. The genus includes the following species: Gunnera albocarpa Gunnera arenaria Gunnera densiflora Gunnera dentata Gunnera flavida Gunnera hamiltonii Gunnera kauaiensis Gunnera magellanica Gunnera magnifica Gunnera manicata Gunnera masafuerae Gunnera monoica Gunnera perpensa Gunnera petaloïdea Gunnera prorepens Gunnera tinctoria Cyanobacterial Symbiosis All Gunnera species form a symbiotic relationship with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, specifically Nostoc punctiforme. The bacteria enter the plant through specialized glands located at the base of each leaf stalk. Once inside, they establish an intracellular symbiosis, providing the plant with fixed nitrogen in exchange for fixed carbon from the plant. This unique intracellular interaction is not observed in other higher plants and offers a potential model for developing novel symbiotic relationships between crop plants and cyanobacteria. Such innovations could enable agricultural growth in nitrogen-deficient soils. Uses The stalks of Gunnera tinctoria (commonly known as nalcas) are edible and are primarily consumed fresh. They are also used in salads, as an ingredient in liquor, or to make marmalade. The leaves of this species are traditionally used in Chilean cuisine to cover curanto, a traditional dish. Additionally, Gunnera perpensa is utilized in Southern Africa as a source of traditional medicine.
